EXAMINATION STRUCTURE
Full Course Examination Architecture
This paper contains 250 continuously numbered, premium practice questions covering all five Big Ideas of AP Computer Science Principles. Questions 1–220 represent authentic multiple choice items, followed by Questions 221–250 comprising 30 comprehensive Create Performance Task Written Response scenarios with full College Board scoring rubrics.
★ Priority Rating System
★★★★★ Very Important
High-frequency exam concepts: Pair programming, Program Purpose vs Function, Binary & Hex conversions, Integer overflow & Round-off, 1-indexed list algorithms, Robot grid paths, Internet open protocols (TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP), Fault tolerance, Public-key cryptography, Algorithmic bias, and Creative Commons licensing.
★★★★ Mandatory
Core computational standards: User input validation, Sampling rate & bit depth, Lossless (RLE, LZW) vs Lossy compression, Nested conditionals, REPEAT UNTIL termination, Procedural abstraction with return values, Parallel speedup & Amdahl's Law, and Multi-Factor Authentication.
★★★ Important
Essential computing standards: Software development lifecycles, Variable swapping mechanics, Modulo arithmetic, Linear vs Binary search efficiency, Trace tables, Packet headers & routing, and Digital footprint privacy.
★★ Foundational
Foundational applications: Code comments, Peer inspection etiquette, Diagnostic tools (Ping, Traceroute), and Public domain copyright dedication.
Course Topic & Unit Weighting Coverage
Unit 1: Creative Development (10%–13% Exam Weight) — Collaboration, Design, Debugging, Documentation
Unit 2: Data Representation (17%–22% Exam Weight) — Binary, Hex, Compression, Overflow, Round-Off, Big Data
Unit 3: Algorithms & Programming (30%–35% Exam Weight) — Variables, Conditionals, Loops, Lists, Procedures, Decidability
Unit 4: Computer Systems & Networks (11%–15% Exam Weight) — Internet, TCP/IP, DNS, Fault Tolerance, Parallel & Distributed Computing
Unit 5: Impact of Computing (21%–26% Exam Weight) — Digital Divide, Bias, Crowdsourcing, IP Licensing, Cybersecurity, Privacy
Create Performance Task (30 In-Depth Scenarios) — Purpose vs Function, Data Abstraction, Algorithms, Testing
AP Exam Pro Tip: Remember three universal AP CSP conventions: (1) In AP pseudocode, lists and strings are strictly 1-indexed (first element is at index 1); (2) A logic error executes to completion without crashing but produces incorrect output silently; and (3) In asymmetric cryptography, messages are encrypted using the recipient's public key and decrypted only with their private key!
• Questions 1–220: Multiple Choice (4 choices A–D, single correct answer), arranged continuously.
• Questions 221–250: Create Performance Task Written Response scenarios (9 points each with full rubrics).
• Master Answer Key: Complete reference matrix for Q1–Q220 with priority star ratings.
• Detailed Worked Solutions: In-depth bullet-point explanations and full distractor analysis for all 250 items.

    }

    }
    RETURN totalFare
}

        {

            IF (accountList[studentIndex] < 5.00)
            {
                sendLowBalanceAlert(studentIndex)
            }
            RETURN true
        }
        ELSE
        {
            logDeclinedCharge(studentIndex, chargeAmount)
            RETURN false
        }
    }
    RETURN false
}
The app calls `processTransaction(accountBalances, 3, 2.50)` when student #3 purchases a lunch item.

The progress evaluation algorithm is encapsulated in procedure `evaluateWeeklyProgress`:
PROCEDURE evaluateWeeklyProgress(stepsList, dailyGoal)
{
    totalSteps <- 0
    daysGoalMet <- 0
    
    FOR EACH dayCount IN stepsList
    {
        totalSteps <- totalSteps + dayCount
        IF (dayCount >= dailyGoal)
        {
            daysGoalMet <- daysGoalMet + 1
        }
    }
    
    avgSteps <- totalSteps / LENGTH(stepsList)
    
    IF (daysGoalMet >= 5 AND avgSteps >= dailyGoal)
    {
        RETURN "Goal Achieved! Outstanding consistency."
    }
    ELSE
    {
        RETURN "Goal Incomplete. Keep pushing next week!"
    }
}

Warehouse Inventory Restock Prioritization Algorithm
Unit 3: Algorithms & Programming ❖ Warehouse Inventory Restock Prioritization Algorithm
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT 9 Points Total
Program Scenario & System Architecture
An e-commerce fulfillment warehouse utilizes an automated inventory robot management system. The system maintains parallel lists tracking items, current stock, and minimum thresholds:
`stockLevels <- [14, 5, 42, 2, 80]`
`reorderLimits <- [20, 15, 30, 10, 50]`
The restocking algorithm scans items and populates a restock queue:
PROCEDURE generateRestockOrders(stock, limits, urgencyFactor)
{
    urgentOrders <- []
    i <- 1
    
    REPEAT LENGTH(stock) TIMES
    {
        currentStock <- stock[i]
        threshold <- limits[i]
        
        IF (currentStock < threshold)
        {
            deficit <- threshold - currentStock
            IF (deficit >= urgencyFactor)
            {
                APPEND(urgentOrders, i)
            }
        }
        i <- i + 1
    }
    RETURN urgentOrders
}

(b) [3 Pts]: Explain the algorithmic logic inside `generateRestockOrders`, detailing how it identifies which items require urgent restocking.
(c) [2 Pts]: Determine the exact list returned when `generateRestockOrders(stockLevels, reorderLimits, 7)` is executed, showing work for each index.
(d) [2 Pts]: Describe what logical error would occur if the instruction `i <- i + 1` was placed inside the inner `IF (deficit >= urgencyFactor)` block instead of at the end of the loop.

PROCEDURE verifyFlightSafety(altitudeList, minAltitude, maxAltitude)
{
    isSafe <- true
    violatingWaypoints <- 0
    
    FOR EACH alt IN altitudeList
    {
        IF (alt < minAltitude OR alt > maxAltitude)
        {
            isSafe <- false
            violatingWaypoints <- violatingWaypoints + 1
        }
    }
    
    IF (isSafe = true)
    {
        RETURN "Flight Path Approved"
    }
    ELSE
    {
        RETURN concat("Safety Violation: Ineligible Waypoints = ", violatingWaypoints)
    }
}

`matchAnswers <- [true, true, true, false, true, true]`
The score calculation algorithm awards base points and streak multipliers:
PROCEDURE computeQuizScore(answerList, pointsPerQuestion, streakBonus)
{
    totalScore <- 0
    currentStreak <- 0
    
    FOR EACH isCorrect IN answerList
    {
        IF (isCorrect = true)
        {
            currentStreak <- currentStreak + 1
            totalScore <- totalScore + pointsPerQuestion
            IF (currentStreak >= 3)
            {
                totalScore <- totalScore + streakBonus
            }
        }
        ELSE
        {
            currentStreak <- 0
        }
    }
    RETURN totalScore
}

Question 1: Pair Programming Roles & Workflows ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — The navigator observes the code being written, considers the broader architectural picture, identifies edge-case defects in real time, and suggests strategic improvements.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• In the formal pair programming paradigm, two programmers share a single workstation (or screen).
• The 'driver' physically controls the keyboard and mouse, focusing on the mechanics of writing syntactically correct code.
• The 'navigator' focuses on the strategic direction, reviewing each line of code as it is typed, checking for logic flaws and boundary bugs, and anticipating upcoming architectural challenges.
• Regularly switching roles between the driver and navigator produces higher-quality code with fewer defects than programming in isolation.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): Typing code and managing the keyboard is the direct responsibility of the 'driver', not the navigator.
✕ (C): Pair programming requires continuous, real-time collaboration; the navigator does not wait until the driver finishes before starting their review.
✕ (D): The navigator actively engages with technical design and algorithmic logic rather than limiting themselves to marketing or administrative documentation.
Question 2: Diversity in Computing & Bias Mitigation ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — Including team members and test groups from diverse demographic backgrounds would have ensured the training dataset and algorithmic parameters accounted for varied facial structures, lighting conditions, and skin tones.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Algorithmic bias frequently arises when software development teams lack diversity and subsequently use narrow, non-representative training datasets or assumptions.
• By collaborating with diverse developers and broad demographic test groups during the investigative and design phases, teams identify blind spots and unrepresentative data samples early.
• College Board Big Idea 1 (CRD-1.C) explicitly emphasizes that consultation and collaboration with diverse stakeholders reduce human bias in computing innovations.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Engineers with identical backgrounds often share the same blind spots; pairing does not remove bias unless diverse perspectives and diverse datasets are intentionally incorporated.
✕ (C): single engineer is highly prone to individual unconscious biases and cannot validate broad demographic compatibility alone.
✕ (D): Testing only on a small, non-diverse corporate group exacerbates selection bias rather than eliminating real-world deployment errors.
AP Computer Science Principles ❖ Worked Solutions & Distractor Analysis Page 129

QUESTIONS 3 – 4 OF 220
Question 3: Asynchronous Collaboration & Version Control ★★★ IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — Using a centralized or distributed version control system (such as Git) with branch management, commit histories, and pull requests.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Asynchronous collaboration occurs when team members work at different times and locations without real-time face-to-face interaction.
• Version control systems provide branch isolation, transparent commit logs, and merge conflict resolution, ensuring multiple developers can contribute concurrently without overwriting files.
• Pull requests allow structured peer review and collaborative feedback before code is integrated into the main production branch.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): Emailing zip archives lacks conflict detection, commit tracking, and granular version history, inevitably causing overwritten code.
✕ (C): Restricting implementation to one person bottlenecking the project is not effective asynchronous collaboration and fails to leverage team capacity.
✕ (D): Merging untracked code at the end of a project produces massive integration conflicts and impossible-to-trace logic bugs.
Question 4: Collaboration in the Software Life Cycle ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — During the investigation and reflection phase when developers interview users to understand their challenges, workflows, and goals.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• The software development life cycle begins with investigation, reflection, and requirement gathering.
• Collaborating with end users, domain experts, and prospective clients during the investigation phase ensures that the program purpose directly solves genuine user needs.
• Failing to collaborate early often leads to building a technically sound program that ultimately fails because it solves the wrong problem.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): ompiling is an automated machine process performed by software compilers, not a phase for user collaboration.
✕ (C): Minification is an automated optimization step for reducing file size and bandwidth, requiring no user requirement discovery.
✕ (D): Post-discontinuation analysis cannot retroactively define or correct the active purpose and requirements of a live system.

QUESTIONS 5 – 6 OF 220
Question 5: Interpersonal Communication & Consensus ★★★ IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — Develop rapid interactive prototypes of both designs and conduct usability testing with representative end users to gather empirical feedback.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Effective collaboration in software development relies on objective consensus building, data-driven decisions, and user-centric evaluation.
• Creating rapid prototypes allows developers to test competing hypotheses directly with target users and measure usability metrics (e.g., task completion time, clarity).
• Empirical user testing resolves subjective disagreements constructively while aligning the software with genuine user requirements.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): Seniority-based overrides stifle innovation, disregard valid usability arguments, and weaken collaborative team dynamics.
✕ (C): eleting core features simply because of a design disagreement harms the final utility of the software.
✕ (D): Minimizing lines of code is a secondary engineering preference that must never take precedence over user accessibility and task fulfillment.
Question 6: Code Reviews & Peer Inspection ★★ FOUNDATIONAL
Correct Answer: (B) — Code reviews allow peers to identify subtle logic errors, enforce consistent coding standards, and share domain knowledge across the team.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Peer code reviews provide a second pair of eyes to spot algorithmic oversights, unhandled boundary conditions, and security vulnerabilities.
• They ensure adherence to institutional style guides, making code readable and maintainable for future contributors.
• They also facilitate mentorship and team knowledge transfer so that no single developer is an irreplaceable single point of failure.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): ode reviews evaluate correctness and architecture; they cannot alter fundamental physical computing constraints or produce zero CPU usage.
✕ (C): ode reviews supplement automated testing; they never replace unit, integration, and regression test suites.
✕ (D): ode reviews occur internally during development and have no impact on compiled binary disassembly or reverse engineering.

Question 7: Pair Programming Failure Modes ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — Both partners must actively participate, communicate continuously, and periodically switch between the driver and navigator roles.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Pair programming succeeds only when both participants actively engage in their respective roles and communicate thoughts aloud.
• The navigator must stay vigilant, reviewing logic, verifying variable names, and thinking ahead.
• Teams should switch roles at structured intervals (e.g., every 15–20 minutes) to keep cognitive fatigue low and engagement high.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): Pair programming is language-agnostic and widely practiced in high-level languages like Python, JavaScript, and Java.
✕ (C): Pair programming by definition involves exactly two developers (a pair); four programmers constitutes ensemble or mob programming.
✕ (D): Frequent incremental testing and running of code is an essential hallmark of agile pair programming.
Question 8: Accessibility & Inclusive Design Collaboration ★★★ IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — Accessibility specialists, screen-reader users, and individuals with varied degrees of visual impairment.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Inclusive design requires collaborating directly with users who have diverse physical and cognitive capabilities.
• Working with screen-reader users and accessibility experts reveals navigation barriers (e.g., missing alt text, poor keyboard tab indexing, low color contrast) that sighted developers often overlook.
• This collaborative testing ensures compliance with universal design standards like WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines).
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): atabase administrators handle server-side storage and have no direct role in front-end assistive technology evaluation.
✕ (C): Low-contrast neon schemes actively impair accessibility for visually impaired and color-blind users.
✕ (D): Network throughput stress testers measure server scaling, not user interface accessibility.

QUESTIONS 9 – 10 OF 220
Question 9: Task Decomposition & Delegation ★★ FOUNDATIONAL
Correct Answer: (B) — Decompose the overall application into distinct, modular components with clearly defined input/output interfaces and assign specific modules to team members.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Modular decomposition breaks a large, complex system into smaller, self-contained modules or procedures.
• By establishing clear interface contracts (what inputs a module expects and what outputs it returns), developers can work on separate modules in parallel without interfering with one another.
• This separation of concerns reduces merge collisions and allows targeted unit testing.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): ssigning identical tasks to multiple programmers without coordination wastes team resources and generates irreconcilable duplicate code.
✕ (C): ommitting directly to the master branch without feature branches causes constant merge conflicts and destabilizes working code.
✕ (D): Lack of documentation prevents collaboration and cripples the team's ability to maintain or integrate code.
Question 10: Collaborative Debugging Strategies ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — Explaining the code forces the programmer to articulate their assumptions step-by-step, which often exposes flawed logic that was previously overlooked.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Explaining code line-by-line to another person (or even an inanimate object like a rubber duck) forces the developer to slow down and verbalize their mental model.
• Discrepancies between what the developer *thinks* the code does and what the code *actually* does become glaringly obvious during this verbal breakdown.
• The collaborator can ask clarifying questions, test edge cases, and challenge unexamined assumptions.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Spoken words have zero physical or compiler-level interaction with software execution.
✕ (C): Replacing a buggy function with an uncontrolled infinite loop introduces severe crashes and demonstrates poor engineering.
✕ (D): The cognitive benefit of verbalizing code logic does not depend on the listener's academic credentials; simply structuring the explanation reveals the flaw.

QUESTIONS 11 – 12 OF 220
Question 11: Program Purpose vs. Program Function ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — The purpose is to encourage environmental sustainability by helping users track carbon savings; the function is how the code accepts transit miles, multiplies by emission constants, and displays the saved kilograms on screen.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• College Board Learning Objective CRD-2.A explicitly distinguishes between program purpose and program function.
• The *purpose* of a program explains *why* the software exists—the real-world problem it solves, the user need it meets, or the creative goal it achieves (e.g., promoting sustainable transit choices).
• The *function* of a program describes *what* the software actually does and *how* it behaves during execution (e.g., reading numeric inputs, executing formulas, updating UI labels).
• Confusing purpose with mechanical function is one of the most common student errors on the AP CSP exam.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): This reverses the two concepts: arithmetic operations are internal functional mechanics, while environmental sustainability is the broader societal purpose.
✕ (C): Purpose and function are fundamentally distinct; purpose is user- and problem-centric, whereas function is behavioral and operational.
✕ (D): Programming syntax and UI color palettes are implementation details, neither of which defines overarching program purpose.
Question 12: Identifying Program Purpose from Context ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — To connect food-insecure families with safe, allergen-compatible groceries efficiently and with dignity.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• The primary purpose of a software system addresses the underlying human or societal problem being solved.
• Here, the program facilitates the safe, anonymous, and efficient distribution of allergen-appropriate food to community members in need.
• Technical operations like HTTP transactions or database querying are mere functional tools to accomplish this human-centered purpose.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): Generating network traffic is a physical operational byproduct, never the purposeful objective of civic software.
✕ (C): Testing database data types describes an engineering technical check, not the reason the pantry deployed the system.
✕ (D): Password security is a routine administrative subsystem, not the primary purpose of the food pantry application.

Question 13: Program Function Behavior ★★★ IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — To evaluate whether cartTotal meets a 50.00 threshold, set shippingFee to either 0.00 or $5.99 accordingly, and compute finalCharge as their sum.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Program function describes the concrete algorithmic behavior of the code when executed with specific inputs.
• This code segment checks a conditional relational expression (cartTotal >= 50.00), branches execution to assign the shipping fee variable, and calculates the total charge via addition.
• This step-by-step operational narrative precisely articulates program function.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): This is an exaggerated, unrelated aspiration that has nothing to do with this code's operational mechanics.
✕ (C): Packaging sustainability is not addressed or influenced by this conditional fee assignment algorithm.
✕ (D): omparing computer speed to human cognition is a philosophical observation, not a description of the code's execution behavior.
Question 14: Impact of User Feedback on Program Purpose ★★★ IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — Broaden the program purpose to include rhythmic physical therapy and iteratively enhance the function by adding large, high-visibility visual pulses and haptic vibrations.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• In modern software development, unexpected user adoption often reveals valuable new program purposes.
• Developers should embrace real-world user feedback by refining the program's scope and iteratively adapting its functionality (e.g., adding accessibility features, larger visual cues, haptic feedback) to meet diverse user needs.
• This iterative responsiveness is a core competency in College Board Big Idea 1 (Creative Development).
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): rtificially restricting eager users undermines software adoption and ignores a high-impact creative opportunity.
✕ (C): eleting working audio functionality destroys the core product rather than improving it.
✕ (D): Punitive pricing drives away users instead of solving accessibility and usability challenges.

QUESTIONS 15 – 17 OF 220
Question 15: Identifying Divergence Between Purpose & Function ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — The program's purpose remains helping students calculate their GPA, but its actual function contains a logic error that prevents it from fulfilling that purpose.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• The *purpose* is the intended goal defined by the developer (calculating GPA for students). A bug in the code does not change what the program was intended to do.
• The *function* is what the code actually does upon execution (in this case, executing subtraction instead of addition due to a logic error).
• Because the functional behavior deviates from the intended purpose, the developer must debug the arithmetic logic.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): The purpose is what the creator intended (which remains valid); it is the function that is malfunctioning.
✕ (C): Programs always have functional behavior (even if flawed) and retain their designer's intended purpose.
✕ (D): ompilers strictly translate code into machine instructions; they possess no human agency to modify program purpose.
Question 16: Creative Expression in Computing ★★ FOUNDATIONAL
Correct Answer: (B) — An interactive generative art installation that renders evolving fractal patterns and harmonious synthesized tones in response to ambient gallery sounds.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Computing is not limited to business automation and mathematics; it is a powerful medium for personal, artistic, and creative expression (CRD-1.A).
• Interactive generative art combining visual fractals, audio synthesis, and microphone responsiveness represents creative computing.
• Payroll scripts, interest calculators, and network latency testers are traditional analytical data processing utilities.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): Interest computation is a standard financial mathematical calculation.
✕ (C): Tax form generation is a routine administrative compliance process.
✕ (D): Network ping testing is a diagnostic systems administration task.
Question 17: User-Centered Design Principles ★★★ IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — Increasing typography contrast and font scale while replacing multi-finger gestures with prominent, single-tap zoom buttons.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• User-centered design tailors the software's functional interface to the specific physical, perceptual, and cognitive needs of its target audience.
• For seniors who may experience reduced visual acuity or dexterity challenges, large high-contrast fonts and simple single-tap target buttons drastically improve usability and reduce frustration.
• Listening to user feedback during prototype testing is essential for creating accessible, effective computing innovations.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): ommand-line interfaces require technical syntax knowledge and would severely degrade usability for everyday users.
✕ (C): Requiring users to memorize coordinates creates an impossible cognitive burden, destroying the app's usefulness.
✕ (D): epleting battery life is a severe performance defect, not a user-centered design improvement.

Question 18: Specifying Requirements & Constraints ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — System specifications and operational constraints that guide program design and validation.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• In professional software engineering, specifications describe *what* the system must accomplish (e.g., latency under 500 ms) and constraints describe the boundaries within which it must operate (e.g., legal privacy standards, memory limits).
• Documenting specifications and constraints during the investigation and design phases ensures the software meets safety, regulatory, and performance thresholds.
• Testing against these specifications validates whether the final program function fulfills its critical purpose.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Ignoring specifications in critical domains like healthcare leads to fatal software failures and legal liabilities.
✕ (C): Specifications are written documentation in natural language, not syntax bugs in source code.
✕ (D): ompiler directives are specific programming language keywords (like #pragma or inline), not high-level system requirements.
Question 19: Social Impact as Program Purpose ★★★ IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — An offline-first educational quiz platform that runs on low-cost refurbished tablets and syncs student progress via local USB drives when internet access is unavailable.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• The 'digital divide' refers to the socioeconomic gap between those who have ready access to computers and high-speed internet and those who do not.
• A lightweight platform that functions offline on inexpensive hardware directly mitigates the digital divide by bringing educational resources to underserved or rural students without reliable broadband.
• High-cost VR setups and paid streaming apps exacerbate the digital divide rather than narrowing it.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): Expensive hardware and high-bandwidth requirements exclude low-income students, widening the digital divide.
✕ (C): ryptocurrency trading bots serve financial markets and have no educational equity purpose.
✕ (D): Usage-based fee models penalize students with limited financial resources.

Question 20: Program Function Validation ★★ FOUNDATIONAL
Correct Answer: (A) — Test the function with varied inputs, including a list with one item, a list where the maximum is first, a list where the maximum is last, and a list with duplicate maximum values.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Verifying program function requires structured testing across varied scenarios, edge cases, and boundary conditions.
• Testing with a single-element list, lists with maximums at the front, middle, and end, and duplicate values confirms that the algorithm behaves correctly regardless of data ordering.
• A single trivial test case (like [5]) cannot expose logic flaws such as off-by-one errors or indexing bugs.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Testing only one trivial case is insufficient to validate algorithmic correctness across general inputs.
✕ (C): Editor syntax highlighting colors have no connection to the mathematical correctness of algorithm execution.
✕ (D): Word processors do not execute source code; changing extensions corrupts file associations.
Question 21: Program Inputs & Sensors ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — The accelerometer and GPS hardware chip transmitting raw coordinate and motion data to the operating system.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Program inputs are data received by a program from users, files, network streams, or physical sensors.
• Accelerometers, GPS receivers, gyroscopes, and optical heart rate monitors are hardware sensors that generate continuous input data streams for software applications.
• Visual screens, audio chimes, and generated PDF reports are outputs, not inputs.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): Information displayed on a screen is a visual output, not an input.
✕ (C): hime sounds played through earbuds are auditory outputs.
✕ (D): Generated emails and PDF reports are persisted digital outputs.

QUESTIONS 22 – 23 OF 220
Question 22: Event-Driven Programming Concepts ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — Code blocks (event handlers) execute asynchronously in response to triggered events, such as user mouse clicks, keystrokes, timers, or incoming network messages.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• In event-driven programming (CRD-2.C), the flow of execution is determined by external events.
• The program registers 'event listeners' or 'event handlers' for specific events (e.g., onButtonClick, onTimerTick, onSensorThreshold).
• When an event occurs, the runtime triggers the corresponding event handler. If the user never clicks a button, that button's click handler never executes.
• This contrasts with classic sequential scripts that run strictly from start to finish without pausing for interactive input.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (A): Strict linear execution describes simple sequential batch scripts, not event-driven interactive applications.
✕ (C): ompilers do not order execution alphabetically; procedures execute when invoked or triggered by events.
✕ (D): PU temperature affects hardware thermal throttling, never the logical scheduling of event handler routines.
Question 23: Identifying Program Outputs ★★★ IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) — The electrical signal triggering the mechanical water pump valve to open and release water.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Program outputs include data displayed to users, data written to files, and physical actuation signals sent to mechanical hardware (actuators).

Question 32: Odd and Even Binary Numbers ★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) — Examine the rightmost bit (least significant bit): if it is 1, the number is odd; if it is 0, the number is even.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• In binary representation, place values are powers of 2: [..., 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1].
• Every place value greater than 2⁰ is an even number (2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ...).
• The sum of any combination of even numbers is always even.
• Therefore, the only bit that can contribute an odd quantity (1) to the total sum is the least significant bit (2⁰ = 1).
• If the rightmost bit is 1, the total value is odd; if it is 0, the total value is even.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

Question 42: ASCII vs. Unicode Comparison ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT

Question 63: Floating-Point Architecture (Sign, Exponent, Mantissa) ★★★ IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — Floating-point numbers can represent an immense range of both extremely large and microscopically small values, but at the cost of potential precision loss and round-off errors.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:

• The exponent allows the binary decimal point to 'float', enabling representation of vast cosmic scales (e.g., 10³⁸) and subatomic scales (e.g., 10⁻³⁸) within 32 or 64 bits.
• However, the mantissa has a fixed number of precision bits (e.g., 53 bits in 64-bit double), meaning numbers with more significant digits than the mantissa must be rounded off.

Question 140: Concurrent Modification / Deletion Bug ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT

• - `-8` moves from index 2 to index 1!
• - `12` moves from index 3 to index 2.
• - `15` moves from index 4 to index 3.
• - New list: `[-8, 12, 15]`.
• - Then `i <- i + 1` increments `i` to 2!
• Iteration 2: Now `i = 2`. The code checks `nums[2]`, which is `12`!
• Notice that `-8` (now at index 1) was completely skipped and never checked!
• Consequently, `-8` remains in the list, causing the algorithm to fail.
• (To fix this bug, one should iterate backwards or only increment `i` when no deletion occurs).

Question 148: Centralized vs. Decentralized vs. Distributed Networks ★★★★ MANDATORY

Question 149: Packet Switching vs. Circuit Switching ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — Packet switching allows multiple devices to dynamically share the same physical network cables simultaneously without reserving dedicated, idle communication channels.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Analyze the fundamental mechanics of packet switching:
• In **circuit switching**, a dedicated physical circuit is reserved exclusively for a call. Even when both parties are silent, the wire cannot be used by anyone else.
• In **packet switching**, data is broken into small chunks called **packets**. Each packet travels independently across shared routers and wires.
• If one channel is quiet, other devices' packets use that bandwidth, dramatically increasing the efficiency, capacity, and scalability of shared physical infrastructure.
• Packets from hundreds of different users interleave across the same transatlantic fiber cable without interference.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Packets can take different paths and arrive out of order; TCP uses sequence numbers in the header to reassemble them.
✕ (C): Reserving an unbroken physical wire for the entire duration is the definition of circuit switching, not packet switching.
✕ (D): Packet switching manages congestion dynamically through buffering and packet dropping, not by forcibly disconnecting users.
Question 150: Function & Role of Network Routers ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — To inspect the destination IP address of each incoming packet and forward it along an optimal path toward its final destination.

• A router is a specialized computing device that connects two or more computer networks.
• When a packet arrives, the router reads the metadata in the packet header—specifically the **destination IP address**.
• The router consults its internal routing table to determine the best next network 'hop' and sends the packet on its way.
• Routers act like postal sorting centers, forwarding packages toward their destination without needing to understand or alter the contents of the payload.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Rendering HTML into visual elements is the job of a client web browser, not a network router.

Question 151: The End-to-End Architectural Principle ★★★★ MANDATORY

Question 158: Structure & Capacity of IPv6 Addresses ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT

• **IPv6** addresses are **128 bits** long.
• Because 128 binary bits would be too long to write in decimal, they are formatted as 8 groups of 4 **hexadecimal digits** separated by colons (`:`).
• Each hexadecimal digit represents 4 bits (8 × 4 × 4 = 128 bits).

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

Question 159: Mathematical Comparison of IPv4 vs. IPv6 Capacity ★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) — 2⁹⁶ times larger (an astronomical factor of approximately 7.9 × 10²⁸ times larger).
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Calculate the exponential growth of binary address spaces:
• The number of possible IPv4 addresses is 2^{32}.
• The number of possible IPv6 addresses is 2^{128}.
• To find how many times larger IPv6 is compared to IPv4, divide the two quantities:
• \frac{2^{128}}{2^{32}} = 2^{128 - 32} = 2^{96}
• Each additional bit doubles the address space. Adding 96 bits doubles the address space 96 times!
• 2^{96} ≈ 7.92 × 10^{28}, which is nearly 80 octillion times larger than the entire IPv4 address space.
• (Common student trap: Dividing 128 by 32 to get 4 completely overlooks that address space grows exponentially in base 2, not linearly).
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): ivides 128 by 32, confusing the bit length ratio with the exponential capacity ratio (2^{128} ≠ 4 × 2^{32}).
✕ (C): Subtracts exponents without applying base 2 (2^{96}, not 96).
✕ (D): alculates 2^4 = 16, which is an incorrect exponent calculation.

Question 161: Time-To-Live (TTL) and Routing Loop Prevention ★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) — Each router decrements TTL by 1; if TTL reaches 0 before the packet reaches its destination, the packet is discarded to prevent it from circulating endlessly in an infinite routing loop.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Analyze the function of the Time-To-Live (TTL) header field:
• In complex mesh networks, temporary routing misconfigurations or table updates can occasionally create routing loops (e.g. Router A sends to Router B, which sends back to Router A).
• To prevent orphaned packets from bouncing back and forth forever and clogging bandwidth, every router that forwards a packet decrements its TTL counter by 1.
• If a packet's TTL counter drops to 0, the current router discards (drops) the packet and sends an error message (ICMP Time Exceeded) back to the sender.
• This acts as a self-destruct mechanism that safeguards network capacity.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): TTL decrements towards zero; it does not increment or grant administrative privileges.
✕ (C): TTL is a packet-level hop counter, not a cellular billing quota meter.
✕ (D): TTL is unrelated to physical hardware thermal sensors.
Question 162: Hierarchical Structure of IP Addresses ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — The leading bits (network prefix) identify the specific network or Internet Service Provider (ISP), while the trailing bits identify the specific host device on that network.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Analyze the hierarchical structure of IP addressing:
• An IP address is split into two primary parts: the **Network ID (prefix)** and the **Host ID (suffix)**.
• Global backbone routers only need to inspect the network prefix to route a packet to the destination's ISP or enterprise network (e.g., University of California or Comcast).
• Once the packet arrives at the local network's gateway router, the local router inspects the host ID to deliver the packet to the exact computer or smartphone.
• This hierarchy prevents routers from having to memorize billions of individual device locations, keeping global routing tables compact and efficient.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): IP addresses identify network interfaces, not device form factors (mobile vs desktop).
✕ (C): IP addresses do not encode raw GPS coordinates.
✕ (D): Random addressing would make routing impossible; hierarchy is essential for scalable packet forwarding.

Question 165: IP Spoofing & Network Security Vulnerabilities ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — An attacker crafts data packets with a falsified source IP address in the packet header to conceal their identity or impersonate a trusted computing device.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:

• Because basic IP packets do not have built-in authentication of the source address in the header, a malicious sender can forge (spoof) the source IP address.
• Uses of IP spoofing:
• - Impersonation: Tricking a server into believing a request comes from an authorized internal device.
• - Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) Amplification: Sending small requests with the victim's spoofed IP address to third-party servers, causing those servers to send massive responses directly to the victim, overwhelming their bandwidth.
• Defenses include ingress filtering at routers and cryptographic authentication.

Question 167: Out-of-Order Packet Arrival & TCP Reassembly ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT

Question 168: Characteristics of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — Connection-oriented and reliable; it establishes a connection, verifies that all packets arrive intact, requests retransmission of lost packets, and reassembles them in order.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Examine TCP's reliability guarantees:
• **TCP** is the primary transport-layer protocol for applications requiring 100% data fidelity.
• Key properties:
• - **Connection-oriented:** Uses a 3-way handshake to establish a synchronized session between sender and receiver.
• - **Reliability:** The receiver sends acknowledgment (ACK) packets for received data.
• - **Retransmission:** If an ACK is not received within a timeout window, TCP assumes the packet was dropped and automatically retransmits it.
• - **In-order Delivery:** Uses sequence numbers to guarantee data is passed to the application in order.

Question 169: Characteristics of the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — Connectionless and lightweight; it transmits packets rapidly with minimal overhead, without establishing a formal connection, tracking packet order, or retransmitting lost packets.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Examine UDP's speed and lightweight design:
• **UDP** prioritizes speed and low latency over perfect reliability.
• Key properties:
• - **Connectionless:** Senders transmit datagrams immediately without waiting for a handshake.
• - **No Acknowledgments:** Receivers do not send ACKs back to the sender.
• - **No Retransmission:** If a packet is corrupted or dropped due to network congestion, UDP simply ignores it and continues.
• - **Minimal Overhead:** Smaller header size (8 bytes vs. TCP's 20+ bytes) and zero round-trip latency delays.

✕ (B): Guaranteed in-order delivery and retransmission describes TCP, not UDP.

Question 170: Application Selection: TCP vs. UDP ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — Application 1 should use TCP (guaranteeing 100% accuracy without data corruption); Application 2 should use UDP (minimizing latency and input lag where dropping an occasional packet is acceptable).
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Analyze protocol trade-offs for real-world application domains:
• **Application 1 (Banking / Financial Transfer):**
• - Absolute data integrity is mandatory. A dropped packet could mean missing digits in a financial account transfer.
• - Waiting a few milliseconds for TCP retransmission is completely acceptable to guarantee 100% accuracy.
• - **Choice: TCP**.
• **Application 2 (Live Multiplayer Gaming / VoIP):**
• - Immediate responsiveness is paramount. If a player's coordinate packet from 100 milliseconds ago is lost, retransmitting it is useless because the player has already moved.
• - Stalling the game to retransmit stale position data causes severe lag/stutter.
• - **Choice: UDP**.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Swaps the protocols; banking cannot afford packet loss, and gaming cannot tolerate TCP retransmission latency.
✕ (C): UDP is heavily utilized worldwide for video streaming (DNS, VoIP, gaming, YouTube, Netflix).
✕ (D): TCP routinely transmits all forms of digital data, including numeric financial transactions.

Question 171: Network Congestion & Packet Dropping Mechanics ★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) — When incoming packets arrive faster than the router's outgoing link can transmit, the router's memory buffer overflows and drops incoming packets; TCP detects missing acknowledgments and retransmits them at a reduced sending rate.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Analyze router queue management and TCP congestion control:
• Routers have finite internal RAM memory buffers (queues) to hold packets waiting for an outgoing line.
• When traffic bursts exceed the outgoing bandwidth, the buffer fills up completely. Any further incoming packets must be discarded (**packet drop**).
• Under TCP, when the sender fails to receive an acknowledgment (ACK) for the dropped packet within a timeout period, it triggers **TCP Congestion Control**:
• - The sender retransmits the lost packet.
• - Crucially, the sender cuts its transmission speed (window size) in half, allowing intermediate routers to clear their backlogs.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Packet dropping is an automatic physical consequence of buffer overflow, not an intentional behavioral penalty.
✕ (C): Routers have finite memory buffers; they cannot store infinite data.
✕ (D): Packet drops are routine everyday occurrences on the Internet; they do not reboot the global backbone.
Question 172: The TCP Three-Way Handshake ★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) — 1. Client sends SYN (Synchronize) 2. Server responds with SYN-ACK (Synchronize-Acknowledge) 3. Client responds with ACK (Acknowledge)
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Trace the 3-Way Handshake protocol steps:
• Step 1: The client initiates the session by sending a **SYN** packet containing its initial sequence number.
• Step 2: The server receives the request, agrees to communicate, and responds with a **SYN-ACK** packet (acknowledging the client's sequence number and stating its own initial sequence number).
• Step 3: The client receives the SYN-ACK and sends back an **ACK** packet, confirming that both sides are synchronized.
• Once this 3-step negotiation concludes, the connection is established and application data transfer begins.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): GET, POST, and DELETE are application-layer HTTP methods, not transport-layer connection establishment signals.
✕ (C): ata transfer only occurs after the handshake is successfully completed.
✕ (D): Ping/Pong are ICMP echo utilities, not the TCP handshake sequence.

QUESTIONS 173 – 174 OF 220
Question 173: Packet Fragmentation & Retransmission Efficiency ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — If a single packet is corrupted or dropped due to network noise, only that individual 1,500-byte packet needs to be retransmitted, rather than re-sending the entire 100 MB file.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Evaluate the error recovery efficiency of packetization:
• In real-world networks, brief interference (microwave noise, radio fading, brief congestion) can corrupt a few bits.
• If a file were sent as one continuous 100 MB block, a single flipped bit at minute 9 would invalidate the entire transfer, forcing the sender to restart all 100 MB from scratch.
• By fragmenting data into small packets (typically bounded by the Maximum Transmission Unit, ~1,500 bytes):
• - Only the specific lost or damaged packet is retransmitted (a fraction of a millisecond of bandwidth).
• - Packets from other users can interleave smoothly, preventing a single large file from monopolizing a physical cable.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Nothing travels faster than the speed of light in vacuum; signals in fiber travel at roughly 67% light speed.
✕ (C): Modern computers routinely store gigabytes of data in RAM and terabytes on disk.
✕ (D): ata charges are based on total bytes transmitted, regardless of packet fragmentation size.
Question 174: Packet Checksums & Bit Error Detection ★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) — To allow the receiving device to perform a mathematical verification to detect whether any bits in the packet were corrupted or altered during transmission.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Analyze error detection using checksums:
• When sending a packet, the sender performs a mathematical calculation (adding up the binary numbers of the header/data) and writes the resulting sum into the **checksum** field.
• When the packet arrives, the receiver executes the exact same mathematical formula on the received bits.
• If the receiver's computed sum matches the header's checksum, the packet is verified as intact.
• If a bit flipped during transmission (due to electrical noise or signal degradation), the sums will not match, alerting the receiver that the packet is corrupted and must be dropped.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): opyright licenses are legal documents, not network error-checking hashes.
✕ (C): hecksums are mathematical bit sums; they do not inspect or categorize advertising content.
✕ (D): hecksums calculate data integrity, not physical geographic distance.
AP Computer Science Principles ❖ Worked Solutions & Distractor Analysis Page 214

QUESTIONS 175 – 176 OF 220
Question 175: Protocol Data Encapsulation Hierarchy ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — The HTTP message is placed inside a TCP segment, which is placed inside an IP packet, which is placed inside an Ethernet frame.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Trace the hierarchical encapsulation process:
• 1. **Application Layer (HTTP):** Generates the application data (e.g. `GET /index.html HTTP/1.1`).
• 2. **Transport Layer (TCP):** Wraps the HTTP data with a TCP header (ports, sequence numbers), creating a **TCP Segment**.
• 3. **Internet Layer (IP):** Wraps the TCP segment with an IP header (source/destination IP addresses), creating an **IP Packet**.
• 4. **Link / Network Interface Layer (Ethernet/Wi-Fi):** Wraps the IP packet with hardware MAC addresses and frame check sequences, creating an **Ethernet Frame**.
• The frame is then encoded into physical electrical voltages, radio waves, or light pulses for transmission.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Reverses the hierarchy; HTTP is high-level application data, while IP is lower-level routing.
✕ (C): Ethernet frames wrap IP packets, not the other way around.
✕ (D): TCP wraps HTTP; HTTP does not wrap TCP.
Question 176: Domain Name System (DNS) Core Role ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — It translates human-readable domain names (such as `www.collegeboard.org`) into machine-readable numerical IP addresses (such as `198.51.100.45`).
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Understand the purpose and function of the Domain Name System (DNS):
• Humans find symbolic, alphabetical names (like `google.com` or `collegeboard.org`) easy to remember and type.
• However, network routing hardware (routers and switches) operates exclusively using numerical binary/dotted-decimal IP addresses.
• DNS acts as the Internet's decentralized, distributed phonebook, taking a requested text hostname and resolving it into its corresponding IP address.
• Without DNS, users would be forced to memorize and enter 32-bit or 128-bit numerical strings for every website.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): ata encryption is handled by security protocols such as TLS/HTTPS, not DNS.
✕ (C): File compression is managed by media codecs and application software, not DNS.
✕ (D): Physical signal transmission is the role of physical layer media (copper cables, fiber optics, radio waves).
AP Computer Science Principles ❖ Worked Solutions & Distractor Analysis Page 215

QUESTIONS 177 – 178 OF 220
Question 177: Hierarchical Architecture of the DNS System ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — Root DNS server → Top-Level Domain (TLD) server (`.org`) → Authoritative DNS server (`collegeboard.org`).
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Analyze the DNS resolution hierarchy:
• 1. **Root DNS Servers:** Direct queries to the appropriate Top-Level Domain (TLD) nameservers based on the extension (`.org`, `.com`, `.edu`).
• 2. **TLD Servers:** Manage the specific domain registry (e.g., all `.org` domains) and provide the address of the authoritative nameserver for that organization.
• 3. **Authoritative Nameservers:** Possess the definitive, canonical database records for that specific domain (`collegeboard.org`) and return the exact IP address for the sub-host (`apstudents`).
• This distributed hierarchy ensures no single server creates a global bottleneck or single point of failure.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): The authoritative server cannot be queried first because its location is not known until resolved by the Root and TLD servers.
✕ (C): This lists physical networking hardware devices rather than the logical hierarchy of DNS name resolution.
✕ (D): TLD servers cannot direct traffic without the Root server identifying the proper registry first.
Question 178: DNS Caching & Time-To-Live (TTL) ★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) — It decreases latency for recurring page visits and significantly reduces network query traffic on upstream DNS root and TLD servers.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Evaluate the performance advantages of DNS caching:
• Without caching, every single HTTP request (including every separate image, CSS file, and script on a web page) would require repeated round-trip DNS lookups across the globe.
• Caching stores the result locally in browser memory or the local recursive resolver.
• This dramatically cuts down lookup latency (from ~50-100 ms to <1 ms) and prevents global root nameservers from crashing under excessive query volume.
• The TTL field specifies when cached records expire so that changes in IP addresses eventually propagate.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Websites frequently update servers and IP addresses; caching simply pauses lookups for the duration of the TTL.
✕ (C): NS caching does not encrypt traffic or protect against eavesdropping.
✕ (D): evices still require an active physical connection to the network to download web content.
AP Computer Science Principles ❖ Worked Solutions & Distractor Analysis Page 216

QUESTIONS 179 – 180 OF 220
Question 179: DNS Spoofing & Cache Poisoning Cyberattack ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — DNS Spoofing (also known as DNS Cache Poisoning).
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Identify the mechanism of DNS Spoofing / Cache Poisoning:
• In **DNS Spoofing**, an attacker feeds invalid, forged DNS response data into a resolver's cache.
• The cache stores the malicious entry for the duration of the TTL.
• When unsuspecting users query that resolver, they receive the attacker's IP address instead of the genuine server.
• The URL bar may appear to display the legitimate domain name, but the browser connects to an attacker-controlled server designed to steal credentials (phishing).
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): oS attacks overwhelm a target server with traffic to render it unavailable; they do not covertly redirect DNS queries.
✕ (C): Severing cables halts connectivity entirely rather than routing traffic to a clone website.
✕ (D): keylogger is software or hardware that records keystrokes on a local machine, not a server cache corruption.
Question 180: Hypertext Transfer Protocol: HTTP vs. HTTPS ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — HTTPS encrypts the data exchanged between the browser and web server using TLS/SSL, preventing unauthorized eavesdroppers on the open Wi-Fi network from reading credit card numbers and passwords.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Distinguish between HTTP and HTTPS:
• **HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol):** Transmits web requests and responses in plain text. Anyone monitoring the local wireless airwaves (packet sniffing) can read passwords, session cookies, and personal data.
• **HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure):** Wraps HTTP communication inside an encrypted layer (Transport Layer Security / TLS or SSL).
• Even if eavesdroppers intercept the packets over open public Wi-Fi, the payload appears as undecipherable cryptographic ciphertext.
• HTTPS also authenticates the web server to ensure users are communicating with the authentic business.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): HTTPS involves cryptographic operations that may consume slight CPU processing, but it has no relationship to battery optimization.
✕ (C): Network protocols cannot protect electronic hardware from electrical power surges.
✕ (D): HTTPS does not double network speed; encryption adds a microscopic computational overhead.

Question 201: Definition of Computing Bias ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) — Computing bias can be embedded directly by human programmer choices, but more frequently emerges when machine learning models are trained on historical datasets that reflect human prejudices or demographic underrepresentation.
Step-by-Step Bulleted Reasoning:
• Analyze the nature of Computing Bias in AP CSP Big Idea 5 (IOC-1.D):
• Computing bias does not require a developer to harbor personal prejudice or intentionally write discriminatory `IF/ELSE` statements.
• Most modern bias arises through **machine learning on historical data**:
• - If society had historical hiring, lending, or policing disparities, feeding those historical records into a machine learning algorithm teaches the algorithm to replicate and codify those exact biases.
• - If certain demographic groups are underrepresented in the training sample, the model learns poor feature representations for them.
• Software reflects the values, assumptions, and data of its creators and historical contexts.
Why Other Options Are Incorrect:
✕ (B): Microprocessor heat relates to physical thermodynamics, not algorithmic fairness.
✕ (C): The belief that algorithms are inherently objective is a dangerous misconception; algorithms learn and amplify human biases present in training data.

Question 221 Solution: Program Purpose, Function, and User Input Processing in a Healthcare App
Unit 1: Creative Development ❖ Program Purpose, Function, and User Input Processing in a Healthcare App
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT 9 Points Maximum
Official AP Exemplary Student Model Response
• (a) Purpose vs. Function:
- The purpose of HydrateHero is to promote student-athlete health and physical well-being by helping users monitor their daily hydration and achieve water intake goals during sports seasons.
- The function describes the algorithmic behavior: reading text from input fields, validating positive numeric format, converting milliliters to ounces, adding to an accumulator variable `dailyTotalOz`, and updating UI labels and progress graphics in real time.
• (b) Inputs & Outputs:
- Input: `rawAmount` entered into `waterAmountInput` (string/number format, e.g., '500') and `unitType` selected from `unitDropdown` (text string: 'oz' or 'ml').
- Output: Text displayed on `dailyTotalLabel` (string showing current total vs. goal), visual update to the circular progress bar, or the auditory `playCelebrationSound()` when reaching the goal.
• (c) Tracing '500 ml' Execution:
- 1. User taps `logButton`, triggering the click event listener.
- 2. `rawAmount` ('500') and `unitType` ('ml') are extracted from the UI controls.
- 3. Condition `(isNumber(500) = true AND 500 > 0)` evaluates to TRUE.
- 4. `convertToOunces(500, "ml")` computes approximately 16.9 ounces.
- 5. `dailyTotalOz` increments by 16.9.
- 6. `updateProgressBar` redraws the fill percentage, and `dailyTotalLabel` is updated.
- 7. If `dailyTotalOz >= dailyGoalOz`, an auditory chime plays.
• (d) Handling '-15':
- Because `-15 > 0` evaluates to FALSE, the boolean expression evaluates to FALSE.
- Execution branches immediately to the `ELSE` block.
- `errorLabel` displays 'Please enter a valid positive number!'.
- Validation Benefit: Without this check, adding a negative number would decrease the athlete's logged water intake, creating a logic error that falsifies daily health records.

• (a) Need for Iterative Development:
- A non-iterative approach assumes all requirements are perfectly known upfront and builds the final software without intermediate validation.
- In this scenario, studio testing by a sighted developer failed to anticipate real-world usage barriers.
- Iterative development allows the developer to deploy early prototypes, observe authentic user friction, and refine the software across repeated cycles based on direct user feedback.
• (b) Proposed Modifications:
- 1. Audio Guidance: Implement computer vision edge-detection that emits auditory beeps or verbal prompts ('tilt camera down', 'page detected') to guide physical framing.
- 2. Playback Controls: Add prominent voice rate controls (0.75x, 1.0x, 1.25x) along with tap-anywhere gestures to pause and rewind speech.
• (c) Next Iterative Cycle:
- Investigate: Consult visually impaired classmates on preferred speech speeds and gesture habits.
- Design: Create a wireframe and gesture map for full-screen touch controls and audio feedback prompts.
- Prototype: Implement the gesture listener and speech rate parameters in an experimental software build.
- Test: Have the three classmates test reading textbook pages in varied ambient lighting, recording success rate and user satisfaction.
• (d) Developer Blind Spots:
- As a sighted person, the developer took visual page orientation and on-screen button locations for granted, assuming users could see to align the camera.
- Failing to consult diverse users early resulted in a system that was technically functional but practically inaccessible to its target audience.

- Trigger Event: A touch or mouse click event on `castVoteButton`.

- Outputs: Visual screen display (`displayConfirmationScreen` or `displayErrorScreen`), physical actuation output (`printPaperReceipt`), and auditory alert (`playSound`).
• (b) Event-Driven vs. Sequential:
- A sequential batch script runs strictly from top to bottom on a predetermined dataset and exits.
- An event-driven kiosk runs continuously in an event loop, remaining idle until a student interacts with the screen. When a touch event occurs, the registered handler executes, returns to idle, and awaits the next student.
• (c) Concurrency & Event Queue:
- When simultaneous votes arrive from Kiosk A and Kiosk B, the central server places them into an incoming FIFO (First-In, First-Out) event queue.
- Each event receives a high-resolution millisecond timestamp.
- The server processes queue items sequentially in atomic transactions: vote 1 is recorded and the student marked voted before vote 2 is processed.
- This prevents race conditions where duplicate ballots or corrupted tally totals could occur.
• (d) Edge Case & Prevention:
- Edge Case: A student leaves `idInput` completely blank ("") or enters letters instead of digits.
- Prevention: Add validation: `IF (length(studentId) = 6 AND isDigitsOnly(studentId))`. If invalid, immediately display 'Invalid Student ID format' before making server database calls.

Question 227 Solution: Binary Sensor Representation & Integer Overflow in a Smart Greenhouse Monitor
Unit 2: Data Representation ❖ Binary Sensor Representation & Integer Overflow in a Smart Greenhouse Monitor
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT 9 Points Maximum
Official AP Exemplary Student Model Response
• (a) Binary to Decimal Conversion:
- Positional place values for an 8-bit byte from left to right: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
- Calculation: (1×128) + (1×64) + (1×32) + (1×16) + (1×8) + (1×4) + (1×2) + (1×1) = 255.
- Therefore, the binary value 11111111₂ equals decimal 255.
• (b) Register Overflow Mechanics:
- Adding 1 to 11111111₂ yields 100000000₂ in standard 9-bit binary arithmetic.
- Because the microcontroller's register is physically constrained to 8 bits, the 9th bit (the 256 place value) cannot fit and is truncated/discarded.
- The 8 bits stored in memory roll over to 00000000₂ (decimal 0). This is an integer overflow error.
• (c) Operational Consequences on Irrigation:
- If the overflow occurs when humidity is near 100% (or raw pulses exceed 255), the control algorithm reads the register as 0%.
- The greenhouse logic will interpret 0% as dangerously dry air and trigger an emergency watering cycle.
- This floods the crops with excessive water, potentially rotting root systems and ruining greenhouse yields.
• (d) Prevention Strategies:
- 1. Wider Data Type: Upgrade the register variable to a 16-bit unsigned integer (`uint16_t`), expanding capacity to 65,535 and preventing overflow.
- 2. Input Clamping / Guard Rails: Add defensive conditional checks in the update routine: `IF (counter >= 254) { counter <- 254 }` to clamp the counter at maximum capacity.

• (a) Continuous Analog vs. Discrete Digital Audio:
- The human voice generates an analog sound wave: a continuous variation in air pressure over time with an infinite number of possible frequencies and amplitudes.
- NoteVoice converts this into digital data by sampling the wave at fixed discrete time intervals and quantizing each voltage reading into a discrete binary number.
• (b) File Size Calculations (10 minutes = 600 seconds):
- Formula: Total Bits = Sampling Rate (Hz) × Bit Depth (bits) × Channels × Time (seconds).
- Configuration Alpha:
8,000 samples/sec × 8 bits/sample × 1 channel × 600 sec = 38,400,000 bits (4.8 Megabytes).
- Configuration Beta:
44,100 samples/sec × 16 bits/sample × 2 channels × 600 sec = 846,720,000 bits (105.84 Megabytes).
• (c) Auditory Quality Differences:
- Sampling Rate: Beta (44.1 kHz) captures frequencies up to ~22 kHz, reproducing crisp high-frequency consonants (s, t, f) naturally, whereas Alpha (8 kHz) caps at 4 kHz, sounding muffled like an old telephone.
- Bit Depth: Beta (16 bits = 65,536 levels) provides high dynamic range with near-zero background hiss, while Alpha (8 bits = 256 levels) introduces noticeable quantization noise.
• (d) Trade-off Recommendation:
- For students on tight cellular data caps, Configuration Alpha (or a mono 16 kHz compromise) is strongly recommended.
- Alpha's file is 22 times smaller (~4.8 MB vs ~105.8 MB), downloading almost instantly without exhausting mobile data, while human speech remains fully intelligible.

Question 229 Solution: Run-Length Encoding vs. Dictionary-Based Lossless Compression in a Hospital Archive
Unit 2: Data Representation ❖ Run-Length Encoding vs. Dictionary-Based Lossless Compression in a Hospital Archive
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT 9 Points Maximum
Official AP Exemplary Student Model Response
• (a) Lossless Definition & Healthcare Imperative:
- A compression algorithm is lossless if the decompressed output is 100% bit-for-bit identical to the original uncompressed input.
- Lossless compression is strictly mandatory in medical archives because lossy compression permanently discards fine detail, which could erase a hairline bone fracture in an X-ray or alter medication dosages in a medical chart, causing fatal diagnostic errors.
• (b) RLE Encoding and Reduction:
- Original string: `BBBBBBBBBBWWWWBBBBBB` (20 characters).
- Run 1: 10 'B's -> `10B`.
- Run 2: 4 'W's -> `4W`.
- Run 3: 6 'B's -> `6B`.
- Compressed string: `10B4W6B` (6 characters without spaces).
- Percentage reduction: (20 − 6) / 20 × 100% = 70.0% reduction (or 65% if formatted with single spaces `10B 4W 6B`).
• (c) Why RLE Succeeds on Category 1 but Fails on Category 2:
- Category 1 (dental scans) features massive contiguous blocks of identical color pixels (hundreds of identical black pixels in empty background space), which RLE compresses into a few bytes.
- Category 2 (English text) contains words where letters rarely repeat consecutively. In English sentences, runs are almost all length 1 (e.g., 'd-o-c-t-o-r' becomes `1d1o1c1t1o1r`), doubling the file size rather than compressing it.
• (d) How Dictionary Compression Handles Category 2:
- Dictionary compression (LZW) searches for multi-character patterns that recur across the document, regardless of whether they are adjacent.
- Phrases like 'patient tolerated procedure well' (32 characters) are assigned a short numeric pointer (e.g., Token #12). Every occurrence is replaced by Token #12.
- Upon decompression, the table reconstructs the exact original clinical phrasing with zero lost information.

Part (b) (b) Correctly encodes `BBBBBBBBBBWWWWBBBBBB` as `10B 4W 6B` (or `10B4W6B` / 6 chars) and calculates reduction: (20 - 6) / 20 = 70% reduction (or 7 chars with spaces = 65%). 3 pt
Part (c) (c) Explains that X-rays feature long contiguous runs of identical pixels which RLE excels at, whereas English text rarely has consecutive identical letters (e.g., 'patient' has runs of length 1), causing RLE to expand text size. 2 pt
Part (d) (d) Explains that dictionary compression identifies multi-word repeated phrases throughout the text, replacing them with compact numeric tokens in a lookup table, preserving exact words bit-for-bit upon decompression. 2 pt

Question 230 Solution: Lossy JPEG Compression & Quality Trade-Offs in an Online School Newspaper
Unit 2: Data Representation ❖ Lossy JPEG Compression & Quality Trade-Offs in an Online School Newspaper
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT 9 Points Maximum
Official AP Exemplary Student Model Response
• (a) Compression Type & Data Fate:
- JPEG is a lossy compression algorithm.
- During conversion, mathematical transformations (Discrete Cosine Transform and quantization) identify and permanently discard subtle color variations and high-frequency edge textures.
- This discarded data is permanently deleted from the file and cannot be recovered.
• (b) Compression Ratio & Space Savings Calculations:
- Compression Ratio: Uncompressed Size / Compressed Size = 25 MB / 1.2 MB ≈ 20.83 : 1.
- Percentage Space Saved: ((25 − 1.2) / 25) × 100% = (23.8 / 25) × 100% = 95.2% storage reduction.
• (c) Psychovisual Principles Exploited by JPEG:
- 1. Luminance vs. Chrominance Sensitivity: Human eyes possess far more rod cells (detecting brightness) than cone cells (detecting color). JPEG preserves luminance detail while heavily subsampling color (chroma subsampling), which the human visual cortex barely notices.
- 2. High-Frequency Insensitivity: The human eye cannot perceive rapid spatial fluctuations in color across tiny distances. JPEG rounds off high-frequency coefficients to zero with minimal subjective loss.
• (d) Artifacts & Irreversibility:
- Artifact: At 5% quality, visible macroblocking (an 8×8 square pixel grid pattern) and blurry 'ringing' halos around sharp edges will appear.
- Irreversibility: The 25 MB original cannot be restored from the 1.2 MB JPEG because the discarded bits were permanently omitted during quantization; decompressing merely renders the approximated data.

QUESTION 233 OF 250 ❖ MODEL RESPONSE & RUBRIC
Question 233 Solution: School Cafeteria Account & Low-Balance Alert System
Unit 3: Algorithms & Programming ❖ School Cafeteria Account & Low-Balance Alert System
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT 9 Points Maximum
Official AP Exemplary Student Model Response
• (a) Data Abstraction & Complexity Management:
- The data abstraction is the list `accountBalances`, which stores floating-point decimal numbers representing dollar balances for enrolled students.
- Managing Complexity: Without a list, the program would require declaring hundreds of individual variables (`balance1`, `balance2`, `balance3`, etc.). Processing transactions would require massive, repetitive `IF-ELSE` chains. The list enables dynamic positional indexing (`accountList[studentIndex]`) that scales effortlessly to any school population without changing the algorithm.
• (b) Procedural Abstraction & Algorithm Implementation:
- Procedure Name & Parameters: `processTransaction(accountList, studentIndex, chargeAmount)`.
- Algorithm Description:
1. Sequencing & Guard Check: Evaluates whether `studentIndex` is within valid list bounds (between 1 and `LENGTH(accountList)`).
2. Selection (Funds Check): Checks `IF (currentBal >= chargeAmount)`. If true, subtracts `chargeAmount` from the student's balance in-place.
3. Nested Selection (Alert): If the updated balance is strictly below $5.00, calls `sendLowBalanceAlert(studentIndex)`. Returns `true`.
4. Alternative Branch (Decline): If funds are insufficient, calls `logDeclinedCharge` and returns `false` without modifying account balances.
• (c) Testing with Different Call Scenarios:
- Call 1 (Sufficient Funds): `processTransaction(accountBalances, 1, 10.00)`.
• Condition tested: `45.50 >= 10.00` evaluates to `true`.
• Result: `accountBalances[1]` updates to 35.50, procedure returns `true`.
- Call 2 (Insufficient Funds): `processTransaction(accountBalances, 3, 10.00)`.
• Condition tested: `3.25 >= 10.00` evaluates to `false`.
• Result: `logDeclinedCharge(3, 10.00)` is triggered, balance remains 3.25, procedure returns `false`.
• (d) Index Bounds Safety:
- In AP CSP 1-indexed lists, attempting to access index 0, negative indices, or an index greater than list length crashes the program with an 'index out of bounds' error.

- Urgency Threshold: Evaluates nested check `IF (deficit >= urgencyFactor)`. If the shortfall is severe enough, `APPEND(urgentOrders, i)` stores the item's index.

- Index 3: stock 42, limit 30 -> stock exceeds threshold. No action.
- Index 4: stock 2, limit 10 -> deficit = 10 - 2 = 8. Condition `8 >= 7` is true! Append 4.
- Index 5: stock 80, limit 50 -> stock exceeds threshold. No action.
- Returned result: `[2, 4]`.
• (d) Infinite Loop Bug Diagnostic:
- If `i <- i + 1` were moved inside `IF (deficit >= urgencyFactor)`, then whenever an item has no deficit (like Index 1 where deficit 6 < 7), `i` would never be incremented.
- On the next loop cycle, the code would re-evaluate Index 1 indefinitely, trapping the program in an infinite loop.

• (a):
- **Program Purpose:** The purpose of `NetGuard` is to protect local school networks from cyberattacks by autonomously inspecting packet headers and blocking unauthorized or hostile incoming network traffic.
- **Program Function:** A network administrator inputs raw packet logs or observes live network capture streams. The program displays an interactive dashboard showing the total packets processed, the number of dropped malicious packets, and real-time alert logs.
• (b):
- **List Identified:** The list is `incomingPackets`, which stores structured packet objects containing fields: `sourceAddress`, `destPort`, `packetSize`, and `payload`.
- **Managing Complexity:** Using `incomingPackets` allows the system to dynamically process an arbitrary number of network packets (from 10 to 100,000) using a single standardized data structure. Without this list, the programmer would need to define individual variables for every single packet (`packet1_ip`, `packet2_ip`, etc.), which would make dynamic iteration, sorting, and live continuous streaming impossible.
• (c):
- **Procedure Header & Parameters:** `filterPacketStream(packetList, blacklistedPrefixes)` takes the list of incoming packet objects and a list of blacklisted network prefixes.
- **Algorithmic Logic:**
- 1. Initialize an empty list `approvedPackets = []`.
- 2. `FOR EACH packet IN packetList:` (Iteration)
- a. Set `isMalicious = false`.
- b. `FOR EACH prefix IN blacklistedPrefixes:`
- - `IF packet.sourceAddress.startsWith(prefix) OR packet.destPort == 23 THEN` (Selection)
- - Set `isMalicious = true`
- c. `IF isMalicious == false THEN`
- - Append `packet` to `approvedPackets`
- d. `ELSE:`
- - Log security alert with packet metadata.
- 3. Return `approvedPackets` (Sequencing and return value).
• (d):
- **Test Call 1 (Legitimate Traffic):**
- - *Arguments:* `filterPacketStream([Packet('192.168.1.50', port=443)], ['10.0.0.', '172.16.'])`
- - *Condition Tested:* Evaluates a secure HTTPS packet on port 443 with a clean IP address not in the blacklist.
- - *Outcome:* `isMalicious` remains `false`; packet is appended to `approvedPackets` and returned successfully.
- **Test Call 2 (Blocked Attack Traffic):**
- - *Arguments:* `filterPacketStream([Packet('10.0.0.99', port=23)], ['10.0.0.', '172.16.'])`
- - *Condition Tested:* Evaluates an insecure Telnet packet on port 23 matching a blacklisted subnet prefix.
- - *Outcome:* `isMalicious` evaluates to `true`; packet is dropped and a security alert is recorded; returns empty list.

• (b):

Without it, hardcoded branching for every possible route combination would require thousands of messy `IF/ELSE` statements.

- **Procedure Header & Parameters:** `findOptimalPath(networkGraph, startNode, endNode, failedLinks)` takes the network map, endpoints, and a list of dead links.

- 1. Initialize `visitedNodes = []`, `priorityQueue = [[startNode, 0, [startNode]]]`.
- 2. `WHILE priorityQueue IS NOT EMPTY:` (Iteration)
- a. Extract path with lowest cumulative latency.
- b. `IF currentNode == endNode THEN` return path (Selection).
- c. `FOR EACH neighbor IN networkGraph[currentNode]:`
- - `IF [currentNode, neighbor] NOT IN failedLinks AND neighbor NOT IN visitedNodes THEN`
- - Calculate new latency and append neighbor to candidate path queue.
- 3. Return `"NO_PATH_AVAILABLE"` if destination cannot be reached.
• (d):
- **Test Call 1 (Bypassing Failed Link):**
- - *Arguments:* `findOptimalPath(meshNet, 'NodeA', 'NodeD', [['NodeA', 'NodeB']])`

- **Test Call 2 (Total Network Partition):**
- - *Arguments:* `findOptimalPath(meshNet, 'NodeA', 'NodeD', [['NodeA', 'NodeB'], ['NodeA', 'NodeC']])`
- - *Condition Tested:* All outgoing links from `NodeA` are in `failedLinks`.

• (a):
- **Program Purpose:** `SmartResolver` speeds up web browsing and conserves network bandwidth by serving domain-to-IP resolutions from a local memory cache before querying global DNS servers.
- **Program Function:** A user enters a website URL. The program searches its cache table. If a valid record exists, it immediately returns the numerical IP; otherwise, it queries the authoritative server and caches the new record.
• (b):
- **List Identified:** `dnsCacheTable`, a list of records where each entry is a list containing `[domainName, resolvedIP, expirationTimestamp]`.
- **Managing Complexity:** Storing DNS entries in a list allows the program to add, update, and evict an arbitrary number of domain mappings dynamically. Without this list, every single website on the Internet would require three dedicated scalar variables, making program maintenance impossible.
• (c):
- **Procedure Header & Parameters:** `resolveDomain(queryDomain, currentTime, dnsCacheTable)` takes the target domain, current system time, and the cache list.
- **Algorithmic Logic:**
- 1. `FOR EACH entry IN dnsCacheTable:` (Iteration)
- a. `IF entry[0] == queryDomain THEN` (Selection - Match)
- - `IF currentTime < entry[2] THEN` (Selection - TTL Valid)
- - Return entry[1] (Cache Hit - immediate return)
- - `ELSE:`
- - Remove `entry` from `dnsCacheTable` (Evict stale record).
- 2. Set `newIP = queryAuthoritativeServer(queryDomain)` (Sequencing - Cache Miss).
- 3. Append `[queryDomain, newIP, currentTime + 3600]` to `dnsCacheTable`.
- 4. Return `newIP`.
• (d):
- **Test Call 1 (Fresh Cache Hit):**
- - *Arguments:* `resolveDomain('collegeboard.org', 1000, [['collegeboard.org', '198.51.100.10', 2500]])`
- - *Condition Tested:* `currentTime (1000)` is less than `expiration (2500)`.
- - *Outcome:* Returns `'198.51.100.10'` immediately in <1 ms without contacting external root servers.
- **Test Call 2 (Expired TTL - Cache Miss):**
- - *Arguments:* `resolveDomain('collegeboard.org', 3000, [['collegeboard.org', '198.51.100.10', 2500]])`
- - *Condition Tested:* `currentTime (3000)` exceeds `expiration (2500)`; record is stale.
- - *Outcome:* Stale record is evicted; authoritative server is queried; returns newly fetched IP and updates cache.
